kurals.tamil:
ஒழுக்கம் விழுப்பந் தரலான் ஒழுக்கம்
உயிரினும் ஓம்பப் படும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Ozhukkam vizhuppam tharalaan ozhukkam
Uyirinum oampap padum.
kurals.meaning: Because right conduct is what raises a person to true excellence, it must be guarded even more carefully than life itself.
kurals.elementary: Think of your good behavior as the most precious treasure you own, even more precious than your own body. It is what makes people trust and respect you, so you protect it more than anything else.
kurals.university: The chapter opens with a deliberately extreme ranking: ozhukkam (conduct, from ozhuku, ‘to proceed along a course’) is to be guarded (ompa) above uyir, life itself. The reason clause, vizhuppam tharalaan (‘because it confers eminence’), grounds the claim in what conduct produces rather than in divine command; bare life, as Pope's rendering notes, is something ‘all men share’, while conduct is what distinguishes. The word ozhukkam frames the first line at both ends, so the verse itself performs the act of guarding. Parimelazhagar reads ozhukkam as the conduct proper to one's station, whereas modern commentators (Varadarasanar, Karunanidhi) make it universal. The idea that some values outrank survival recurs widely, from Socrates' refusal to weigh life against right action to the rabbinic rule that certain sins must be refused even on pain of death.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The rule of conduct is transcendent law, whether it be taught in the revealed texts or in the sacred tradition; hence a twice-born man who possesses regard for himself, should be always careful to (follow) it.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu calls ācāra, the rule of conduct, the highest law, and tells anyone with self-respect to follow it with constant care.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it puts conduct at the top of all values and asks that it be guarded vigilantly.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong match on conduct as supreme and needing constant care; Manu does not explicitly rank it above life.

christianity.quote_or_event: “be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.”
christianity.explanation: The risen Christ tells the church at Smyrna to stay faithful even if it costs them their lives, and promises a crown in return.
christianity.tie_back: Both place faithful conduct above survival and attach a reward of eminence (a ‘crown’ in one, vizhuppam in the other) to it.
christianity._accuracy_note: Faithfulness under persecution rather than general moral conduct; the ranking above life matches well.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet is reported to have said that he was sent to perfect (complete) good character.
islam.explanation: In this saying, the Prophet describes the whole purpose of his mission as bringing good character to completion.
islam.tie_back: Both treat conduct and character as the central human good, though the hadith does not rank it above life.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, because the page could not be retrieved for verbatim checking. It matches on the primacy of character but not on the ‘above life’ ranking.

judaism.quote_or_event: The rabbis ruled that for three transgressions (idolatry, forbidden sexual relations and murder) a person must accept death rather than commit them: yehareg ve'al ya'avor, ‘let him be killed and not transgress.’
judaism.explanation: Jewish law normally lets almost any commandment be set aside to save life, but for these three core wrongs it requires a person to give up life instead.
judaism.tie_back: This puts into law the Kural's claim that some conduct must be guarded even above life.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close structural match: conduct ranked explicitly above life, but limited to three cardinal sins rather than conduct in general.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Better it is to live one day virtuous and meditative than to live a hundred years immoral and uncontrolled.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha measures a life by its virtue, not its length. One good day is worth more than a century of bad conduct.
buddhism.tie_back: Both value conduct over the mere continuation of life.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Direct comparison of virtue against lifespan; very close in spirit.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Antigone buries her brother Polyneices against King Creon's decree, knowing the penalty is death, because she holds the unwritten laws of the gods above her own survival.
greek_mythology.explanation: Antigone would rather die doing what is right than live by breaking a sacred duty.
greek_mythology.tie_back: She guards right conduct above her life, just as the Kural asks.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Tragic drama, not myth proper. The conduct here is religious duty to the dead rather than everyday decorum.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “a man who is good for anything ought not to calculate the chance of living or dying; he ought only to consider whether in doing anything he is doing right or wrong”
philosophy.explanation: At his trial, Socrates says a good person does not weigh survival at all. The only question is whether an action is right.
philosophy.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural's ranking: right conduct first, life second.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close match on ranking conduct above life; Socrates frames it as right vs. wrong action rather than decorum.

kurals.tamil:
பரிந்தோம்பிக் காக்க ஒழுக்கம் தெரிந்தோம்பித்
தேரினும் அஃதே துணை.
kurals.transliteration:
Parindhoambik kaakka ozhukkam therindhoambith
Therinum aqdhe thunai.
kurals.meaning: Guard your conduct with care, even when it costs you effort. Weigh every other option, and you will find that conduct alone is the companion that truly stays with you.
kurals.elementary: Imagine testing every toy, game and friend to find the one that will stay with you forever. Valluvar says that after checking everything, the one thing that never leaves you is being good, so take good care of it.
kurals.university: Two phrases of care frame the couplet: parindhu ompi kaakka (‘guard it, cherishing it even through pain’) and therindhu ompi therinum (‘even after examining and weighing all’). The second line sounds almost empirical. After surveying the alternatives (wealth, learning, kin, other virtues), one finds that conduct is the only thunai, companion or support. Parimelazhagar and Pappaiah gloss thunai as the aid that goes with a person into this life and the next, which ties the couplet to a widespread image: good conduct is the one thing that ‘goes with’ a person at death. Karunanidhi stresses bearing hardship to keep it. Aristotle offers a close philosophical parallel when he calls virtuous activity more lasting than even scientific knowledge.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “For in the next world neither father, nor mother, nor wife, nor sons, nor relations stay to be his companions; spiritual merit alone remains (with him).”
hinduism.explanation: Manu says every human tie falls away at death, and only the merit a person has built by right living goes on with them.
hinduism.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural's ‘it alone is the companion’: after every alternative is weighed, conduct is what remains.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near-exact image of conduct/merit as the sole lasting companion.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Take fast hold of instruction; let her not go: keep her; for she is thy life.”
christianity.explanation: The father in Proverbs tells his son to hold on to moral instruction and never let it go, because it is life itself.
christianity.tie_back: It shares the Kural's language of guarding and holding fast to the discipline of right living.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on guarding; the ‘only companion after examining all’ element is absent.

islam.quote_or_event: “When carried to his grave, a dead person is followed by three, two of which return (after his burial) and one remains with him: his relative, his property, and his deeds follow him; relatives and his property go back while his deeds remain with him.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet says that of everything that follows a person to the grave, only their deeds stay with them.
islam.tie_back: This matches the Kural's claim that conduct is the one true companion.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close image of deeds as the only lasting companion.

judaism.quote_or_event: “when a man passes away there accompany him neither gold nor silver, nor precious stones nor pearls, but Torah and good deeds alone”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Yose ben Kisma turns down a fortune because only Torah and good deeds go with a person when they die.
judaism.tie_back: Both identify right conduct as the companion that outlasts every other possession.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close match; it pairs good deeds with Torah study rather than conduct alone.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Good is virtue until life's end, good is faith that is steadfast, good is the acquisition of wisdom, and good is the avoidance of evil.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha praises virtue (sīla) that is kept all the way to the end of life.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats virtue as something to be guarded for a whole lifetime.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Matches on lifelong guarding; the ‘sole companion’ idea is only implicit.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Prodicus' fable of the Choice of Heracles, Virtue offers the young hero a hard road but calls herself a faithful helper and ally in labor, in peace and in war, while Vice offers only easy pleasures.
greek_mythology.explanation: Heracles is shown that Virtue is a companion who stays with you through every hardship.
greek_mythology.tie_back: After comparing the alternatives, the chooser finds virtue to be the one reliable companion, as in the Kural's second line.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Allegory rather than myth proper; the companion theme and the comparison of alternatives both fit.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “no function of man has so much permanence as virtuous activities (these are thought to be more durable even than knowledge of the sciences)”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that virtuous activity is the most stable and lasting thing a human being can have, more lasting even than knowledge.
philosophy.tie_back: Both conclude, after comparison, that conduct is the most dependable human possession.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 1.10, 1100b (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close on durability and comparative superiority; ‘companion’ imagery absent.

kurals.tamil:
ஒழுக்கம் உடைமை குடிமை இழுக்கம்
இழிந்த பிறப்பாய் விடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Ozhukkam udaimai kudimai izhukkam
Izhindha pirappaai vidum.
kurals.meaning: Having right conduct is what makes a person nobly born. Falling away from it turns one's birth into a low one.
kurals.elementary: Coming from a ‘good family’ is not about your last name. If you act kindly and honestly, you are from a good family. If you behave badly, it is as if you did not come from a good family at all.
kurals.university: Kudimai (lineage, the dignity of one's house) is redefined here in terms of behaviour. Possessing ozhukkam is itself nobility of birth, while izhukkam (lapse, slipping) ‘becomes’ (aai vidum) a base birth. The verb matters: a lapse does not just disgrace one's family, it converts one's birth into a low one after the fact. Commentators differ on scope. Parimelazhagar and Pappaiah tie conduct to the duties of one's station, a view that fits a varna framework, while Varadarasanar and Karunanidhi read the couplet as a universal critique of status by birth. Either way, it belongs to a long Indian debate, also voiced by the Buddha in the Vasala Sutta and by Yudhishthira in the Mahabharata, over whether birth or behaviour makes a person noble.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When the boy Satyakama Jabala admits that his mother does not know who his father was, the sage Gautama accepts him as a Brahmin student. He reasons that only a true Brahmin would speak such an unflattering truth.
hinduism.explanation: Satyakama's honesty, not his known lineage, proves his worth and earns him entry to Vedic study.
hinduism.tie_back: As in the Kural, conduct (here truthfulness) is what establishes noble standing.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Narrative paraphrase. The story shows conduct establishing status; the negative half (lapse degrades birth) is not illustrated.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And think not to say within yourselves, We have Abraham to our father: for I say unto you, that God is able of these stones to raise up children unto Abraham.”
christianity.explanation: John the Baptist warns the religious elite that descent from Abraham means nothing without repentance and good fruit.
christianity.tie_back: Both reject lineage as a substitute for conduct.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on rejecting pedigree; the context is repentance before judgment.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allāh is the most righteous of you.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an says tribes and lineages exist so that people may know one another, but true nobility is measured by righteousness.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural's redefinition of nobility almost word for word.
islam._accuracy_note: Direct match: nobility is relocated from lineage to righteous conduct.

judaism.quote_or_event: “a mamzer who is a Torah scholar precedes a High Priest who is an ignoramus”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah sets out an order of precedence by birth, then overturns it: a person of the most stigmatized birth who is a scholar outranks the highest-born priest who is ignorant.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, personal attainment overrides the rank one is born into.
judaism._accuracy_note: The overriding criterion is Torah learning rather than conduct, so the match is on the structure (merit over birth) rather than the content.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not by birth is one an outcast; not by birth is one a brahman. By deed one becomes an outcast, by deed one becomes a brahman.”
buddhism.explanation: Called an outcast by a Brahmin, the Buddha answers that high and low status are made by one's actions, not by birth.
buddhism.tie_back: This states both halves of the Kural: good conduct makes one noble, misconduct makes one low.
buddhism.source: Vasala Sutta, Sutta Nipata 1.7, v. 21 (tr. Piyadassi Thera)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on both halves of the couplet.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The nobly born suitors of Ithaca eat up Odysseus' household with insolence and abuse the disguised king, while the slave swineherd Eumaeus shows him true hospitality. The suitors end in death and disgrace.
greek_mythology.explanation: In the Odyssey, the aristocrats behave basely and the lowly servant behaves nobly.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Conduct, not birth, shows who is truly noble, as the Kural claims.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Illustrative narrative rather than an explicit doctrine; the contrast is implicit.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca argues that philosophy does not look at pedigree, and that a hall full of ancestral busts does not make a nobleman. Only the soul (animus) makes a person noble, and it can rise above any condition of birth.
philosophy.explanation: For Seneca, virtue is open to slave and aristocrat alike, and nobility belongs to the character, not the family tree.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the same relocation of nobility from lineage to conduct.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, because the text was not verified verbatim for this entry. The thematic match is strong.

kurals.tamil:
மறப்பினும் ஓத்துக் கொளலாகும் பார்ப்பான்
பிறப்பொழுக்கங் குன்றக் கெடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Marappinum oththuk kolalaagum paarppaan
Pirappozhukkam kundrak kedum.
kurals.meaning: A Brahmin who forgets the Vedas can learn them again. But if he falls away from the conduct that befits his birth, the birth itself is ruined.
kurals.elementary: If you forget your spelling words, you can study them again. But if you become a bully, no amount of studying fixes that. You lose something that is much harder to get back.
kurals.university: This couplet is the chapter's sharpest test case. The paarppaan (Brahmin) is the figure whose status depends most on birth and learning. Valluvar concedes that forgotten Vedic learning (oththu) can be recovered, but if pirappozhukkam, the conduct attached to that birth, declines (kundra), the birth itself is ruined (kedum). The logic is asymmetric: knowledge is a stock that can be replenished, while character is a foundation whose collapse brings down everything built on it. Commentators split between reading the couplet as upholding Brahmin duty (Parimelazhagar, Pappaiah) and as ranking birth below conduct (Karunanidhi). It closely echoes Manu 1.109, where a Brahmin who departs from the rule of conduct ‘does not reap the fruit of the Veda’, and Yudhishthira's answer to the Yaksha in the Mahabharata.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “It is neither birth, nor study, nor learning, that is the cause of Brahmanahood, without doubt, it is behaviour that constitutes it. One's behaviour should always be well-guarded, especially by a Brahmana.”
hinduism.explanation: Asked by the Yaksha what makes a Brahmin, Yudhishthira rules out birth and study and names conduct alone. He adds that a Brahmin in particular must guard it.
hinduism.tie_back: This is nearly the same argument as the Kural: study is secondary, and conduct is what preserves Brahmin standing.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Section 311 (Yaksha Prashna), tr. K. M. Ganguli
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match, even including the specific case of the Brahmin and the word ‘guarded’.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And though I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries, and all knowledge; and though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says that even perfect knowledge counts for nothing without love.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ranks sacred knowledge below the quality of one's conduct.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches on knowledge vs. character; lacks the ‘knowledge is recoverable, conduct is not’ asymmetry and the birth theme.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet taught that the person whose deeds hold him back will not be carried forward by his lineage.
islam.explanation: Noble descent cannot make up for a lack of good deeds.
islam.tie_back: This fits the Kural's claim that a high birth is ruined when conduct fails.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, because the translation was not verified verbatim. Strong match on birth failing without deeds.

judaism.quote_or_event: “anyone whose deeds exceed his wisdom, his wisdom is enduring, but anyone whose wisdom exceeds his deeds, his wisdom is not enduring.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa teaches that learning only lasts when it rests on deeds.
judaism.tie_back: Both rank conduct above learning and warn that learning without conduct collapses.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match on deeds over learning; the birth-status element is absent.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There are brahmans born in the family of preceptors, kinsmen of (veda) hymns. They are often seen committing evil deeds. In this life itself they are despised, in the next they are born in an evil state of existence. High birth does not prevent them from falling into a woeful state, or from censure.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha points to Brahmins of Vedic families who do evil, and says their birth cannot save them from contempt.
buddhism.tie_back: It is the same case as the Kural, a Vedic Brahmin undone by misconduct despite his birth.
buddhism.source: Vasala Sutta, Sutta Nipata 1.7, vv. 25–26 (tr. Piyadassi Thera)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close: both concern Vedic-born Brahmins whose birth is nullified by conduct.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Achilles, son of a goddess and pupil of the wise centaur Chiron, drags Hector's corpse day after day. Apollo protests to the gods that Achilles has destroyed pity and has no shame, and the gods intervene against him.
greek_mythology.explanation: Neither divine birth nor the finest education protects Achilles from the gods' anger once his conduct becomes shameful.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This echoes the Kural: high birth and learning are undone by a lapse in conduct.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Illustrative parallel; Achilles recovers his standing by returning the body, so the ‘ruin’ is not permanent.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Boethius, through Lady Philosophy, argues that nobility is only praise earned by one's ancestors' merits. If it has any good at all, it lies in obliging the nobly born not to fall short of their ancestors' virtue.
philosophy.explanation: Noble birth carries no worth of its own; it only puts the heir under an obligation of conduct.
philosophy.tie_back: This matches the Kural: birth keeps its value only while the matching conduct is kept up.
philosophy.source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy III, prose 6
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, because the text was not verified verbatim. The thematic match on birth depending on conduct is strong.

kurals.tamil:
அழுக்கா றுடையான்கண் ஆக்கம்போன்று இல்லை
ஒழுக்க மிலான்கண் உயர்வு.
kurals.transliteration:
Azhukkaaru udaiyaan-kan aakkampoandru illai
Ozhukkam ilaan-kan uyarvu.
kurals.meaning: Just as prosperity never settles on the envious, true eminence never comes to a person without right conduct.
kurals.elementary: A jealous kid spends so much time being upset about what others have that he never enjoys his own things. In the same way, someone who behaves badly never really rises high, no matter what.
kurals.university: The couplet works by analogy (ponru, ‘just as’). Azhukkaaru, envy, is so incompatible with aakkam (increase, prosperity) that its absence is proverbial, and uyarvu (elevation, rank) is just as surely absent from a person without ozhukkam. Envy gets a whole later chapter (17). Pappaiah reads uyarvu as ‘high lineage’, keeping the chapter's theme of birth, while Varadarasanar reads it as elevation in life generally. The pairing of envy with misconduct is deliberate: Tamil ethics treats envy as the model inner corruption that eats away at outward fortune, which a later couplet (Kural 168) develops. The claim is about incompatibility more than reward: certain dispositions cannot coexist with certain goods.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Seeing the splendour of the Pandavas' palace and the wealth brought to Yudhishthira's Rajasuya sacrifice, Duryodhana is consumed by envy. That envy drives him to the rigged dice game, which ends in the destruction of his whole line.
hinduism.explanation: In the Mahabharata, envy of another's prosperity sets off Duryodhana's moral collapse and his eventual ruin.
hinduism.tie_back: Duryodhana has birth and wealth, yet envy and misconduct keep true eminence from him, as the Kural predicts.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva (Dyuta Parva), tr. K. M. Ganguli
hinduism._accuracy_note: Narrative paraphrase. It illustrates both halves of the analogy (envy and misconduct leading to loss).

christianity.quote_or_event: “For where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work.”
christianity.explanation: James warns that envy breeds disorder and every kind of wrongdoing.
christianity.tie_back: Both treat envy as corrosive and incompatible with anything good growing.
christianity._accuracy_note: Captures envy's destructiveness; does not state the envy/conduct analogy.

islam.quote_or_event: “Avoid envy, for envy devours good deeds just as fire devours fuel or (he said) ‘grass.’”
islam.explanation: The Prophet compares envy to fire that burns up whatever good a person has stored.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes envy the thing that consumes a person's gains.
islam._accuracy_note: Thematic match is good, but Sunnah.com lists this hadith as graded Da'if (weak) by al-Albani.

judaism.quote_or_event: “envy, lust and [the desire for] honor put a man out of the world.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Elazar Ha-kappar names envy first among the traits that destroy a person.
judaism.tie_back: Both see envy as ruining one's place in the world.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong on envy's ruinous effect; the paired claim about conduct is implied.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not by mere eloquence nor by beauty of form does a man become accomplished, if he is jealous, selfish and deceitful.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says jealousy and deceit cancel out every outward advantage.
buddhism.tie_back: This echoes the Kural's point that the envious and ill-conducted cannot reach true eminence.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close match: jealousy and bad conduct block true accomplishment.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Minerva sends Invidia (Envy) to poison Aglauros, who is consumed by jealousy of her sister's good fortune with Mercury. When she tries to block the god's way, she is turned to stone.
greek_mythology.explanation: Envy eats Aglauros from the inside and leaves her with nothing, frozen and ruined.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This vividly shows the Kural's premise that envy and prosperity cannot coexist.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong illustration of the envy half of the analogy; the conduct half is implicit.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza defines envy as a form of hatred that makes a person pained at another's good fortune and glad at their misfortune. For him, every such sad passion lessens a person's power of acting.
philosophy.explanation: Envy is not only unpleasant but actually weakens the one who feels it.
philosophy.tie_back: This helps explain why the Kural says the envious cannot prosper.
philosophy.source: Spinoza, Ethics III, Definitions of the Emotions 23
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. A theoretical explanation of envy's self-harm rather than a direct parallel to the conduct/eminence claim.

kurals.tamil:
ஒழுக்கத்தின் ஒல்கார் உரவோர் இழுக்கத்தின்
ஏதம் படுபாக் கறிந்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Ozhukkaththin olgaar uravoar izhukkaththin
Edham padupaak karindhu.
kurals.meaning: The strong-minded never slacken in their conduct, because they know the harm that follows a lapse.
kurals.elementary: A smart bike rider always wears a helmet, not because they are scared, but because they know how badly a fall can hurt. Strong people keep behaving well for the same reason: they know what happens when you don't.
kurals.university: Uravor, ‘the strong’, refers to strength of mind rather than of body (uram means firmness or resolve). Their steadiness is not naive. It rests on knowing (arindhu) the edham (fault, harm, calamity) that falls on those who lapse. That makes the couplet an argument about moral knowledge: firmness comes from seeing consequences clearly. Olkaar (‘they do not bend or slacken’) suggests constant, everyday vigilance rather than heroic resistance to one temptation. Pappaiah adds that they hold on ‘even when it is hard’ and reads the harm as loss of standing. Many traditions picture true strength as self-mastery: Ben Zoma's ‘Who is mighty?’, the Buddhist rock unshaken by the storm, and Odysseus binding himself because he knows what the Sirens do.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Yama teaches Nachiketas that the good (śreyas) and the pleasant (preyas) both come to a person. The wise one examines them and chooses the good, while the fool, out of greed, chooses the pleasant and falls short of the goal.
hinduism.explanation: Wisdom lies in seeing where each path leads and holding firmly to the good one.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural's uravor, the wise stay steady because they understand the cost of the other path.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. A strong match on discernment grounding firm choice; it is less explicit about the harm of lapse.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says he disciplines himself constantly because he knows he could fall and be disqualified.
christianity.tie_back: This is the same logic as the Kural: steady discipline driven by awareness of the danger of lapsing.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close match on vigilance motivated by knowledge of the danger.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet taught that the strong person is not the one who overpowers others in wrestling, but the one who controls himself when angry.
islam.explanation: Real strength is inner mastery, not physical force.
islam.tie_back: This fits the Kural's word uravor: strength means holding firm in one's conduct.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, because the page could not be re-read for verbatim checking. It matches on redefining strength as self-control.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is mighty? He who subdues his [evil] inclination”
judaism.explanation: Ben Zoma defines the mighty person as the one who masters their own impulses.
judaism.tie_back: This is the same redefinition of the ‘strong’ that the Kural's uravor implies.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match on strength as self-mastery; the ‘knowing the harm’ motive is not stated.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as a storm cannot prevail against a rocky mountain, so Mara can never overpower the man who lives meditating on the impurities, who is controlled in his senses, moderate in eating, and filled with faith and earnest effort.”
buddhism.explanation: The disciplined person is compared to a mountain that no storm can move.
buddhism.tie_back: Both picture the firm person who never gives way.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good image of steadfastness; the motive of foreseeing harm is less explicit.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Warned by Circe that the Sirens' song lures sailors to their death, Odysseus has his crew plug their ears and has himself bound to the mast so that he cannot give in.
greek_mythology.explanation: Knowing the danger in advance, Odysseus arranges things so that he cannot slip.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural: firmness grounded in knowing exactly what harm a lapse would bring.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Close match on foreknowledge of harm producing firm resistance.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato's image of the soul as a charioteer with two horses, the charioteer must keep a firm grip on the unruly dark horse, which always pulls toward what is shameful, if the soul is not to be dragged down.
philosophy.explanation: Reason must hold desire steady at every moment, or the whole soul falls.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's uravor are like the firm charioteer who never loosens the reins.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Allegorical parallel on constant self-restraint; the Kural's social-consequence element is absent.

kurals.tamil:
ஒழுக்கத்தின் எய்துவர் மேன்மை இழுக்கத்தின்
எய்துவர் எய்தாப் பழி.
kurals.transliteration:
Ozhukkaththin eydhuvar menmai izhukkaththin
Eydhuvar eydhaap pazhi.
kurals.meaning: Through right conduct people rise to greatness. Through a lapse in it they earn a disgrace they never needed to suffer.
kurals.elementary: When you are kind and honest, people look up to you. When you cheat or lie, you get a bad name, and it is a bad name you could easily have avoided.
kurals.university: The couplet is built as a strict parallel: ozhukkaththin eydhuvar menmai / izhukkaththin eydhuvar eydhaap pazhi, ‘by conduct they attain eminence; by lapse they attain unattainable blame’. The paradoxical phrase eydhaap pazhi (‘blame that should not be attained’) is read in different ways: as undeserved, as unbearable, or as blame one had no need to incur. Pope's ‘censures undeserved’ takes the first reading, and most modern commentators take the last. Either way, the couplet makes the social stakes of conduct explicit, because menmai (eminence) and pazhi (blame) are verdicts passed by others. Here the chapter moves from inner firmness (136) to public consequence. The same pairing appears in Sanskrit dharmashastra, in the rabbinic ‘crown of a good name’, and in Hesiod's steep path to excellence.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “For a man of bad conduct is blamed among people, constantly suffers misfortunes, is afflicted with diseases, and short-lived.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu lists the results of bad conduct, and public blame comes first.
hinduism.tie_back: This spells out the second half of the Kural: a lapse brings disgrace among people.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close on the blame half; the preceding verse (4.156) supplies the positive half.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The memory of the just is blessed: but the name of the wicked shall rot.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs sets the lasting honour of the righteous against the rotting reputation of the wicked.
christianity.tie_back: Its two-part structure (honour through goodness, disgrace through wickedness) matches the Kural's parallel lines.

islam.quote_or_event: “Nothing is heavier on the believer's Scale on the Day of Judgment than good character. For indeed Allah, Most High, is angered by the shameless obscene person.”
islam.explanation: Good character carries the greatest weight, while shameless conduct draws God's displeasure.
islam.tie_back: Both set honour through good conduct against disgrace through bad conduct.
islam._accuracy_note: Matches the two-part contrast, but the verdict is divine judgment rather than social reputation.

judaism.quote_or_event: “There are three crowns: the crown of Torah, the crown of priesthood, and the crown of royalty, but the crown of a good name supersedes them all.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Shimon ranks a good name, earned by conduct, above learning, priesthood and kingship.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes eminence (menmai) the fruit of conduct.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong on the positive half; the disgrace half is absent.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “But the fragrance of the virtuous blows against the wind. Truly the virtuous man pervades all directions with the fragrance of his virtue.”
buddhism.explanation: The good name of a virtuous person spreads everywhere, even against the wind, which no flower's scent can do.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's first half: conduct brings a widely recognised eminence.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Badness can be got easily and in shoals: the road to her is smooth, and she lives very near us. But between us and Goodness the gods have placed the sweat of our brows: long and steep is the path that leads to her, and it is rough at the first”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod tells his brother that vice is easy to reach, while excellence has to be climbed to by effort.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Both contrast the high standing won by virtue with the low road of vice.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 287–291 (tr. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Contrasts the two paths but stresses effort more than reputation.

philosophy.quote_or_event: At the close of the Republic, Socrates argues that in the long run the just are honoured by gods and men. The unjust are like runners who start fast and fail at the finish, ending in contempt and disgrace.
philosophy.explanation: Over time, justice brings honour and injustice brings public disgrace.
philosophy.tie_back: This mirrors both halves of the Kural's parallel.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. A close match on the honour/disgrace contrast.

kurals.tamil:
நன்றிக்கு வித்தாகும் நல்லொழுக்கம் தீயொழுக்கம்
என்றும் இடும்பை தரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Nandrikku viththaagum nallozhukkam theeyozhukkam
Endrum idumbai tharum.
kurals.meaning: Good conduct is the seed from which good things grow. Bad conduct brings sorrow, always.
kurals.elementary: Plant an apple seed and you get an apple tree. Plant weeds and you get weeds. Being good is like planting a good seed, because nice things grow from it. Being mean only grows trouble.
kurals.university: The farming metaphor vittu (seed) makes nallozhukkam generative. Good conduct is not the good itself but the cause from which good (nandri, here ‘benefit’ or ‘virtue’ rather than ‘gratitude’, though one modern commentator reads it that way) grows over time. Its opposite, theeyozhukkam, gives idumbai (distress) endrum, ‘always’, which suggests a continuous harvest rather than a single punishment. Pappaiah extends the fruit to this life and the next (immai, marumai), which aligns the couplet with karmic causation, while Karunanidhi keeps it within this life. The seed image is nearly universal, from Paul's ‘whatsoever a man soweth’ to the Upanishadic ‘as he acts, so he becomes’ and Aristotle's view that character arises from like activities.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “according as he acts and according as he behaves, so will he be:--a man of good acts will become good, a man of bad acts, bad. He becomes pure by pure deeds, bad by bad deeds.”
hinduism.explanation: Yajnavalkya teaches that what a person does shapes what they become.
hinduism.tie_back: Both say conduct is the seed of what follows: good grows from good, and evil brings its own results.
hinduism.source: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.4.5 (tr. F. Max Müller, SBE 15)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong match on conduct as causal seed; the Upanishad speaks of becoming, the Kural of fruits (good vs. sorrow).

christianity.quote_or_event: “For he that soweth to his flesh shall of the flesh reap corruption; but he that soweth to the Spirit shall of the Spirit reap life everlasting.”
christianity.explanation: Paul uses sowing and reaping to show that the kind of life a person plants decides what they harvest.
christianity.tie_back: It shares the Kural's seed metaphor and its two-sided outcome.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near-exact image: sowing good conduct vs. bad yields opposite harvests.

islam.quote_or_event: “Have you not considered how Allāh presents an example, [making] a good word like a good tree, whose root is firmly fixed and its branches [high] in the sky?”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an compares a good word to a deep-rooted tree that keeps bearing fruit.
islam.tie_back: It shares the Kural's image of goodness as something that grows from a seed or root.
islam._accuracy_note: Matches the organic-growth image; it concerns a ‘good word’ (often read as faith) rather than conduct as such.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For one commandment leads to another commandment, and transgression leads to another transgression; For the reward for performing a commandment is another commandment and the reward for committing a transgression is a transgression.”
judaism.explanation: Ben Azzai teaches that good and bad deeds each multiply their own kind.
judaism.tie_back: Both describe conduct as self-propagating, with good bearing good and bad bearing bad.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close on the generative logic; lacks the explicit seed image.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Mind precedes all mental states. Mind is their chief; they are all mind-wrought. If with an impure mind a person speaks or acts suffering follows him like the wheel that follows the foot of the ox.”
buddhism.explanation: Actions done with a corrupt mind bring suffering that follows as surely as a cart wheel follows the ox.
buddhism.tie_back: This echoes the Kural's second half: bad conduct always brings sorrow. The next verse (Dhp 2) gives the good half.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close match on inevitable suffering from bad conduct; together with v. 2 it covers both halves.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “He does mischief to himself who does mischief to another, and evil planned harms the plotter most.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod warns that wrongdoing comes back on the one who does it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This matches the Kural's claim that bad conduct brings sorrow to its doer.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 265–266 (tr. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Covers only the negative half; lacks the seed image.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Thus, in one word, states of character arise out of like activities.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that repeated acts build up into a settled character of the same kind.
philosophy.tie_back: Conduct is the seed of character, as the Kural's vittu suggests.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 2.1, 1103b (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong on the generative principle; the Kural's focus is on outcomes (good vs. sorrow) rather than character formation.

kurals.tamil:
ஒழுக்க முடையவர்க்கு ஒல்லாவே தீய
வழுக்கியும் வாயாற் சொலல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Ozhukkam udaiyavarkku ollaave theeya
Vazhukkiyum vaayaal solal.
kurals.meaning: People of right conduct cannot bring themselves to speak evil words, not even by a slip of the tongue.
kurals.elementary: Some people are so used to being kind that even when they are angry or surprised, mean words just don't come out. Being good becomes so natural that it even protects your mouth.
kurals.university: The key word is vazhukkiyum, ‘even when slipping’ or ‘even by inadvertence’. Valluvar does not say the disciplined hold back evil speech by effort. He says it is ollaa for them, impossible or unfitting: conduct has become so much second nature that even an unguarded moment is safe. This is a strong claim about habituation, close to Aristotle's view that the virtuous person does the right thing with pleasure and without inner struggle. Tamil ethics gives speech special attention, with chapters on sweet speech (10) and on avoiding useless speech (20). Parallel traditions do too: the Gita counts truthful, non-distressing speech as an austerity, rabbinic ethics condemns lashon hara, and Buddhism places right speech on the Eightfold Path.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Words that do not cause distress, are truthful, inoffensive, and beneficial, as well as regular recitation of the Vedic scriptures—these are declared as austerity of speech.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna names speech that never wounds as a form of spiritual discipline.
hinduism.tie_back: Both treat freedom from harmful speech as a mark of disciplined character.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Matches the ideal of harmless speech; lacks the Kural's ‘even by slip’ point about second nature.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells believers that no corrupt word should come from their mouths at all.
christianity.tie_back: Both require that no evil speech escape a person of good conduct.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close in content; framed as a command rather than as a description of settled character.

islam.quote_or_event: “anybody who believes in Allah and the Last Day should talk what is good or keep quiet.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet makes good speech, or silence, a sign of real faith.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes clean speech a direct expression of inner character.
islam._accuracy_note: Close match on speech as the test of character.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Keep thy tongue from evil, and thy lips from speaking guile.”
judaism.explanation: The Psalmist names guarding the tongue as the path to a good life, a verse central to the later Jewish laws against lashon hara (evil speech).
judaism.tie_back: Both make freedom from evil speech a core part of right conduct.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close in content; the Kural's ‘even inadvertently’ nuance is not present.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who utters gentle, instructive and truthful words, who imprecates none — him do I call a holy man.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha includes gentle, truthful speech that curses no one among the marks of a holy person.
buddhism.tie_back: Both treat blameless speech as the sign of perfected conduct.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong match on speech as a mark of character.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Queen Niobe boasts that her fourteen children make her greater than the goddess Leto, who has only two. Apollo and Artemis kill her children, and Niobe, frozen in grief, is turned to stone.
greek_mythology.explanation: One arrogant speech brings total ruin on Niobe.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is the reverse image of the Kural: the harm that evil words bring.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Illustrates the danger of wrong speech rather than the ideal of never uttering it.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus advises being silent for the most part, or saying only what is necessary in few words, and avoiding talk that is vulgar or that speaks ill of others.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic sage controls speech as part of a disciplined character.
philosophy.tie_back: This matches the Kural's picture of the well-conducted person whose tongue does not slip into evil.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, because the text was not verified verbatim. A good match on disciplined speech.

kurals.tamil:
உலகத்தோடு ஒட்ட ஒழுகல் பலகற்றும்
கல்லார் அறிவிலா தார்.
kurals.transliteration:
Ulagaththoadu otta ozhugal pala-katrum
Kallaar arivilaa thaar.
kurals.meaning: People who have not learned to live in harmony with the world are ignorant, however many books they have studied.
kurals.elementary: Someone could read every book in the library, but if they cannot get along with people, share, or be polite, they have not really learned the most important lesson.
kurals.university: The chapter closes on a paradox: pala-katrum kallaar, ‘having learned much, they have not learned’. What they lack is ulagaththoadu otta ozhugal, conduct that ‘sticks to’ or fits with the world. Commentators differ on what ‘the world’ means. Parimelazhagar and Varadarasanar take it as the worthy (uyarndhor). Pappaiah boldly reads it as adapting the old ethical texts to present circumstances and dropping what no longer fits, which turns the couplet into almost a charter for moral reasoning over rote rule-following. On any reading, social wisdom is the test of learning. This echoes the rabbinic principle that derech eretz (right conduct) comes before Torah, and Aristotle's scorn for people who ‘take refuge in theory’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Professors and pupils, in fact, all who study the scriptures, if addicted to wicked habits, are to be regarded as illiterate wretches. He only is learned who performeth his religious duties.”
hinduism.explanation: Yudhishthira tells the Yaksha that scholars without good conduct are really unlearned, and that only right action makes a person learned.
hinduism.tie_back: This is nearly identical to the Kural's ‘having learned much, they have not learned’.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Section 311 (Yaksha Prashna), tr. K. M. Ganguli
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on the learned-yet-ignorant paradox; Yudhishthira's standard is religious duty rather than social harmony.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes people who keep studying but never reach real understanding.
christianity.tie_back: It captures the Kural's paradox of much learning without true knowledge.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches the paradox; the missing element in Paul is truth, not social conduct.

islam.quote_or_event: “The example of those who were entrusted with the Torah and then did not take it on is like that of a donkey who carries volumes [of books].”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an compares those who carry scripture without living by it to a donkey loaded with books.
islam.tie_back: This is the same point as the Kural: knowledge carried but not lived counts as no knowledge at all.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match on learning without practice being worthless.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Where there is no Torah, there is no right conduct; where there is no right conduct, there is no Torah.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah makes learning and derech eretz (proper conduct in the world) depend on each other.
judaism.tie_back: Both hold that learning without right conduct in the world is empty.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close: derech eretz is literally ‘the way of the land/world’, echoing the Kural's ‘harmony with the world’.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Much though he recites the sacred texts, but acts not accordingly, that heedless man is like a cowherd who only counts the cows of others — he does not partake of the blessings of the holy life.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares the learned person who does not practice to a herdsman counting cattle he does not own.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's paradox exactly: much learning, no real gain.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close match on learning without practice.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod names Eunomia (Good Order), with her sisters Dike (Justice) and Eirene (Peace), as a daughter of Zeus and Themis. She personifies the lawful harmony that holds human communities together.
greek_mythology.explanation: For the Greeks, living in well-ordered harmony with the community was itself a divine gift.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This loosely matches the Kural's ideal of conduct in harmony with the world.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Weak match. No Greek myth directly makes the learned-yet-ignorant point; this is the best available image of social harmony.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But most people do not do these, but take refuge in theory and think they are being philosophers and will become good in this way, behaving somewhat like patients who listen attentively to their doctors, but do none of the things they are ordered to do.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle mocks people who think that studying ethics makes them good without practising it.
philosophy.tie_back: Both hold that learning without conduct is not real knowledge.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 2.4, 1105b (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close match on theory without practice.
